KEY MESSAGE 1

Low pressure will track across the Great Lakes today and into
Northern New York this evening. A warm front will lift north
across the area and produce a few showers or a thunderstorms
this morning mainly across Central NY, but showers may dip as
far south as the Southern Tier. After the warm front passes
there will likely be some clearing for this afternoon.
Temperatures this afternoon will have potential to reach 80
across portions of the Finger Lakes Region and portions of the
Southern Tier. Clouds could linger across the north with
additional showers and thunderstorms possible within the
vicinity of the warm front, generally along the I90 Corridor and
northward. There remains a Marginal Risk (level 1 of 5 ) for an
isolated strong or severe storm across northern areas today, 
with the greatest potential being for isolated damaging wind 
gusts. Instability will reach close to 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE, but
could be higher if more clearing occurs across the north, and 
bulk shear should be close to 40 kts. Models have shifted
shower and thunderstorm chance a little further north for today
and Binghamton on southward into NEPA should remain mostly dry.

It is interesting to see an EML plume move into the region late
tonight and cross during the overnight hours. Mid level lapse 
rates around 8C, but by the time it gets here there is likely 
nothing to kick off storms to tap into these steeper lapse 
rates, as the shortwave will likely be east of the region by 
then. However, this could be something to watch, especially if 
upstream convection gets going. Latest 0Z HRRR does show a 
cluster of showers or thunderstorms overnight into tomorrow 
morning fizzling by the time it makes it into Western NY.
Although latest CAMs guidance appear to indicate that any 
elevated thunderstorms overnight is unlikely, this will
certainly be something to monitor throughout the day. 

KEY MESSAGE 2

No significant changes for the middle of the week. A cold front
eventually pushes through on Wednesday and a moist west-
northwest flow takes hold over the area. A few light showers
will be possible during the afternoon hours. Otherwise, 
Wednesday will be partly sunny to mostly cloudy with highs in 
the 60s to around 70 for CNY, and low to mid-70s in NE PA. 

A much drier air mass and stronger surface high pressure center 
finally reaches the area for Thursday. This should bring plenty of 
sunshine, lower humidity and comfortable temperatures in the upper 
50s to mid-60s. Northwest winds could be a little breezy Wednesday 
night into Thursday morning behind the departing front.

KEY MESSAGE 3

The pattern remains active and our next impactful system pushes
in Thursday night through Friday. This system will likely be followed
by a deep upper trough settling over the Northeast U.S. into 
Saturday. Widespread rain showers will be possible again 
Thursday night through Friday as a fast moving low pressure 
system crosses the region. This system will be followed by a 
deep upper trough/low diving into the area from central Canada.

No major changes in the forecast for this period as the trough 
has been modeled consistently now between most of the major 
global models for the last several runs. Forecast confidence 
continues to increase for lake effect snow this Saturday, but
confidence on if and where it will accumulate is still quite
low. T850 could dip as low as -8C to -10C over Central NY on 
Saturday as cold air advection takes hold on NW flow. Lake 
America water temperatures are quite warm, ranging in the upper 
50s to low 60s. Such a large difference in air and water 
temperatures should produce a decent lake response and our first
lake effect rain and snow event of the season is possible if 
this forecast pattern takes shape. The lake effect precipitation
looks to taper off fairly quickly by later Saturday as high 
pressure moves in.

At this time, with most of the lake effect snow falling during
the daytime hours, the current thinking is that an elevation 
dependent wet snow accumulation could occur, but there remains a
lot of uncertainty in just how cold boundary layer temperatures
will be, especially with the higher sun angle for mid October. 
Current data shows highs in the upper 30s to low 40s Saturday 
afternoon, so snow accumulations will be difficult, but not
completely out of the question if an organized band of heavy
snow can produce rates high enough to overcome the warm surface
temperatures. This is still something to watch very carefully,
because even a heavy wet 2 - 3 inches could cause some issues
with the trees still having all their leaves.

High pressure returns for Sunday and Monday next week. This will 
bring sunny skies and a return to seasonable temperatures during the 
day time. Overnight lows will be cold Saturday night in the mid-20s 
to low 30s areawide, bringing the first widespread freeze to some 
locations.
